Adaptive DWT action tokens vs FAST on π₀-FAST: LoRA training report

Generated 2026-11-19 20:45 by scripts/write_training_report.py from measured run logs and evaluation files. Every number below is measured on the listed hardware unless explicitly marked otherwise. No dataset content is included.

DWT fixed plan @ 2000 steps53/60 = 0.8895% CI [0.78, 0.94], 3 seeds × 20 episodes
DWT adaptive @ 2000 steps39/60 = 0.6595% CI [0.52, 0.76], 3 seeds × 20 episodes

training time per 2000-step run1.82 GPU-hNVIDIA RTX A6000, ≈3.25 s/step

Three ways of turning a 10-step robot action chunk into tokens were fine-tuned with an identical LoRA recipe on one LIBERO task and compared by closed-loop success in simulation. With the same steps and the same GPU time, the fixed-plan DWT beat the FAST baseline at every checkpoint from 1000 steps on, and adaptive DWT overtook FAST from 1500 steps on. The FAST baseline peaked at 1000 steps and then declined, while almost all of its generated streams were malformed (they did not decode to exactly 70 DCT coefficients).

A fourth variant, added afterwards as a control, keeps FAST's transform (DCT) but drops BPE and uses the DWT runs' quantizer, vocabulary and grammar-constrained decoding. It reached 43/60 at 2000 steps, between FAST (17/60) and fixed-plan Haar DWT (53/60), with no malformed streams. Most of FAST's gap is therefore the token format (BPE and free decoding); the transform accounts for a smaller but still measurable part (paired tests in section 4: Haar beats DCT at 1000 and 2000 steps, p < 0.05 uncorrected).

Single-seed follow-ups (section 6): adding BPE to Haar DWT cut success to 9/20, and the mixed sym4→haar wavelet reached 15/20 with 100 tokens per chunk, so neither beats plain Haar at 10-step chunks. A zero-shot probe on nine new objects (section 7) finds that none of the single-task policies generalizes (0–13% success).

Changing only the loss on Haar fixed (section 6b): soft labels plus weighting by coefficient scale reached 52/60 at 2000 steps over 3 seed(s) against 53/60 with plain cross-entropy, same token count: no significant difference, and slower learning in mid-training.

On all 40 LIBERO tasks (section 7b, same 400 episodes for every model) the best model so far is DCT, no BPE · epoch 3 (plain cross-entropy) at 89.2%, against 89.8% for LeRobot's fully fine-tuned π₀-FAST LIBERO. The best Haar DWT fixed model reached 79.2% (Haar DWT fixed, plain from scratch · epoch 2, plain cross-entropy). With the same plain cross-entropy DCT without BPE beats Haar at every epoch, the reverse of the single-task result, and soft labels + full step weighting slowed Haar down. Most of the remaining gap is on the long LIBERO-10 tasks.

3. Training curves (learning-curve runs, seeds 0–2)

The step-like drops in training loss sit at multiples of 365 steps, one pass over the 5840 training windows at batch 16 (365, 730, 1095, 1460, 1825): each new epoch revisits windows already seen, a sign of memorization. Seeds are almost indistinguishable in training loss.

Held-out token loss rises after roughly 1000 steps for every variant: with 40 demonstrations the adapters start to memorize them. It does not predict closed-loop success (next section), and losses are not comparable across variants because the vocabularies and stream lengths differ.

6. Follow-up: which part of the token format matters? BPE, transform, wavelet (seed 0)

The FAST baseline always used BPE (it is part of FAST), while the DWT runs above did not, so the FAST-vs-DWT gap mixes the transform (DCT vs wavelet) with BPE. Single-seed runs with the identical recipe separate them: Haar DWT with BPE, and FAST's DCT without BPE (same quantizer, vocabulary and grammar-constrained decoding as DWT). A third run swaps Haar for the mixed sym4→haar wavelet that won the offline wavelet test at 32-step chunks (section 9), fixed plan, no BPE. Same base model, task, seed 0 and initial states as above.

BPE hurts DWT. With BPE the Haar DWT policy reached 9/20 at 2000 steps against 16/20 without it (and 2/20 vs 16/20 at 1000 steps), although streams were shorter (54 vs 69 tokens) and generation faster (910 vs 1138 ms). Held-out loss per chunk was about 20% higher with BPE: each merged token fixes several coefficient values at once and is drawn from a 4× larger vocabulary. Early checkpoints also spelled coefficients out instead of using merges (67 tokens per chunk at 250 steps). One seed.

DCT without BPE reached 15/20 at 2000 steps, against 16/20 for Haar without BPE and 4/20 for FAST (DCT with BPE), same seed. It was then repeated with seeds 1 and 2 and appears as a fourth variant in sections 3–5.

sym4→haar does not beat Haar at 10-step chunks. It reached 15/20 at 2000 steps against 16/20 for Haar, but learned more slowly and less steadily (0, 0, 12, 6, 15 of 20 at 250, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 steps). At this length sym4 needs symmetric padding, so its streams are 100 tokens instead of 69 and generation is slower (1529 vs 1138 ms), as the offline check predicted. Its offline advantage is at 32-step chunks, which no policy has been trained on yet. One seed.

An offline sweep (scripts/quant_sweep.py) found that coarser rounding of the detail coefficients plus a compact stream would bring DWT + BPE to about 29 tokens per chunk at FAST's error (FAST: 25). That run was dropped in favour of the DCT control above; see the experiment trail.

6b. Follow-up: the loss on Haar DWT fixed

Every run above trains with one-hot cross-entropy, which treats all action tokens alike and every wrong bin alike. Haar is orthonormal, so a coefficient error adds its square to the trajectory error (Parseval), and a one-bin miss costs one quantizer step. Those steps differ about 30× across levels (0.041–0.119 for the coarsest coefficient, 0.0037–0.0142 for the finest details, which are half of the 60 coefficient tokens). Two losses use this, with the same tokens, recipe, seed and decoding as Haar fixed: scale-weighted multiplies each coefficient token's cross-entropy by its step, normalized to mean 1 (≈1.8–5.2 for the coarsest coefficients, 0.16–0.62 for the finest); soft labels + scale-weighted also replaces the one-hot target by q(b) ∝ exp(−((b − b*)·step)² / 2σ²) with σ = 0.007, so a neighbour bin gets real credit at the finest level and almost none at the coarsest. Structure and gripper tokens are unchanged, and the logged losses stay plain cross-entropy. Soft labels + weighting was run with seeds 0–2, weighting alone with seed 0 only.

Neither loss beats plain cross-entropy. Soft labels + weighting reached 52/60 at 2000 steps over 3 seeds against 53/60 for plain (paired: 6 episodes won only by soft labels, 7 only by plain, p = 1.000). Its seed-0 score of 20/20 was the best single run here but did not repeat (20, 18, 14 of 20 for seeds 0, 1, 2). It also learns more slowly in mid-training (behind plain at 1000 and 1500 steps, p ≈ 0.09 and 0.12), as expected from targets that no longer reward the exact bin; its held-out exact-bin accuracy stays about 2 points below plain. Weighting alone (one seed) is within noise of plain at every step. Token count and latency are unchanged and motion is about as smooth. Plain cross-entropy stays the default; soft labels + weighting was nevertheless chosen for the full-LIBERO run, where its slower start matters less over 14,500 steps.

7. Zero-shot generalization to new objects (seed 0)

Every model above was trained on one instruction only. As a first generalization probe, the seed-0 step-2000 checkpoints were run on the other nine libero_object tasks: the same scene type and basket, a different object to pick up, and the new instruction in the prompt. Five initial states per task were drawn at random (seed 0) from states 0–19, a different draw per task and the same states for every model; 45 episodes per model. Nothing was trained on these tasks.

All models fail almost everywhere: every success of every model is on butter or chocolate pudding, and the successful episodes are about as long as a successful alphabet-soup episode (≈145 steps). The likeliest reading is that the policies replay the motion learned on the training task and succeed where the named object happens to be reachable that way, rather than following the new instruction; no videos were recorded, so this is not confirmed. Roughly as on the training task, the Haar fixed policies lead and adaptive is lowest, but the loss changes do not carry over: soft labels + weighting, best on the training task, scores the same as plain cross-entropy here, and the three Haar fixed losses are within one episode of each other. Haar fixed beats Haar DWT adaptive (p = 0.03) in the paired test (uncorrected, one seed); the other differences are not significant. A real generalization test needs multi-task training.

7b. Full LIBERO: all 40 tasks, accuracy per epoch

Every result above is on one task. To compare with published π₀-FAST numbers, Haar DWT fixed was trained once on all of lerobot/libero (40 tasks in four suites, 1,525 training demos, 232,282 windows, codec and normalization refitted) with the same LoRA recipe (rank 16, 20.85 M trainable parameters, effective batch 16, peak lr 2·10⁻⁴, warmup 300; one epoch = 14,500 steps). The schedule was extended as the run went: epoch 1 under a 29,000-step cosine, epochs 2–3 under 43,500 steps (resumed, lr stepped up from 1.1·10⁻⁴ to 1.6·10⁻⁴), and epoch 4 under 58,000 steps, branched three times from the epoch-3 checkpoint with a different loss each (lr 4.6·10⁻⁵ decaying to 2·10⁻⁵). Epochs 1–3 used soft labels + scale weighting. The DCT control (no BPE, plain cross-entropy) repeats exactly this learning-rate history from scratch, and so does a plain-cross-entropy Haar run (2 epochs) that separates the transform from the loss. Later runs test a gentler √step weighting on DCT (one epoch from the plain DCT epoch-2 checkpoint, one epoch from scratch) and an orthogonal-polynomial tokenizer (the best basis in the synthetic token-shift and fingerprint studies) with the same weighting from scratch. Every model is evaluated on the same 400 episodes: all four suites, every task, initial states 0–9, suite-default step limits (Spatial/Object 280, Goal 300, LIBERO-10 520). LeRobot's lerobot/pi0fast-libero (full fine-tune on all of LIBERO) was evaluated by us, unmodified, on the same episodes.

Haar DWT fixed: epoch 1 53.0%, epoch 2 69.0%, epoch 3 75.8%; epoch 4 from the epoch-3 checkpoint: plain cross-entropy 76.2%, scale-weighted 77.0%, soft labels + scale-weighted 74.2%. π₀-FAST LIBERO: 89.8%. DCT without BPE (control): epoch 1 77.0%, epoch 2 85.5%, epoch 3 89.2%. DCT with √step weighting (coefficient-token loss × step0.5, normalized to mean 1; DCT weights 0.56–2.8 instead of 0.25–6.4 for full step weighting): epoch 3 from epoch 2 88.2%. Haar with plain cross-entropy from scratch: epoch 1 58.5%, epoch 2 79.2%.

Transform, same plain cross-entropy: epoch 1: DCT vs Haar 77.0% vs 58.5%, 91 vs 17 episodes won alone, p = 2.1e-13; epoch 2: DCT vs Haar 85.5% vs 79.2%, 51 vs 26 episodes won alone, p = 0.0059. DCT learns faster and stays ahead, the reverse of the single-task result.

Loss on Haar: epoch 1: plain vs soft + weighted 58.5% vs 53.0%, 74 vs 52 episodes won alone, p = 0.061; epoch 2: plain vs soft + weighted 79.2% vs 69.0%, 75 vs 34 episodes won alone, p = 0.00011. Soft labels + full step weighting slowed Haar down; plain Haar after two epochs is already level with every soft or weighted Haar model after three or four.

√step weighting on DCT, one epoch from the plain epoch-2 checkpoint: 88.2% vs 85.5%, 37 vs 26 episodes won alone, p = 0.21 against its starting point, LIBERO-10 80.0% vs 66.0%, 23 vs 9 episodes won alone, p = 0.02; against plain DCT epoch 3 (same start, schedule and epoch, plain loss): 88.2% vs 89.2%, 24 vs 28 episodes won alone, p = 0.68; against π₀-FAST LIBERO: 88.2% vs 89.8%, 29 vs 35 episodes won alone, p = 0.53.

The soft + weighted Haar run rose steeply over the first epochs, then its fourth epoch changed nothing for any of the three losses (paired p ≥ 0.3 against each other and against epoch 3). Its validation token loss bottomed out around the end of epoch 1 (≈2.02) and rose to 2.12 by the end of epoch 3 while the training loss kept falling, so the adapter increasingly fits the training demos; closed-loop success still improved until epoch 3. Most of every model's gap to the fully fine-tuned π₀-FAST LIBERO lies in LIBERO-10 (long, two-step tasks), where errors accumulate over up to 520 steps. One seed and 10 episodes per task (95% interval about ±4 points on the overall rate); the standard LIBERO protocol uses 50.

9. Wavelet choice (offline selection test)

The main models use Haar (db1). An offline test compared 26 transforms (20 standard wavelets and mixed transforms that use a different wavelet at each level, each in periodization and symmetric mode) by the coefficient tokens needed to match FAST's reconstruction accuracy on held-out windows. Top 6 plus common wavelets for reference; full results, rate–distortion curves and basis-shape plots in wavelet_selection.html.

Token counts here exclude gripper and structure tokens and use whole-window transforms, so they are not the deployed codec's counts. This measures how compactly each transform represents the motion, not how well a policy learns its tokens. Of the alternatives, only sym4→haar has been trained, at 10-step chunks where it has no offline advantage (section 6).

10. Caveats

  • Sections 1–7 use one task and one instruction, and the zero-shot probe on nine new objects (section 7) mostly fails for every model. The multi-task results (section 7b) are one seed with 10 episodes per task; nothing here covers other robots.
  • 20 episodes per checkpoint and 3 seeds: confidence intervals are wide, and the paired tests are not corrected for multiple comparisons.
  • The FAST baseline learns LIBERO FAST tokens through the same small LoRA budget. Its low value-token accuracy and malformed streams suggest part of the gap is how hard BPE tokens are to adapt under this recipe; the fully fine-tuned reference shows FAST itself can solve the task. This was tested directly: adding BPE to DWT made it much worse (one seed, section 6), and removing BPE from DCT made it much better (three seeds, sections 4–5).
  • Training is not bit-reproducible: rerunning seed 0 did not exactly reproduce the pilot because of nondeterministic GPU kernels.
  • Models are LoRA fine-tunes, not full fine-tunes; the base model stays frozen.

11. Reproduce

cd smooth-operator/experiment/adaptive_dwt_vla
PY=~/miniconda3/envs/smooth-operator-vla/bin/python
$PY scripts/prepare_libero.py                 # index + train/val split (downloads lerobot/libero)
bash scripts/run_learning_curve.sh 0 1 2      # 9 runs × 2000 steps + checkpoint evals (≈24 h on one A6000)
bash scripts/run_variant.sh dct_fixed 0        # follow-up runs: dwt_fixed_bpe, dct_fixed (seeds 0-2), dwt_fixed_s4h, dwt_fixed_lw, dwt_fixed_slw
bash scripts/run_generalization.sh 0 dwt_fixed dwt_fixed_s4h dct_fixed dwt_adaptive dwt_fixed_lw dwt_fixed_slw   # section 7
bash scripts/run_full_libero.sh dwt_fixed_slw  # section 7b, epoch 1; then STEPS=43500 STOP=29000 and STOP=43500 for epochs 2-3
bash scripts/run_full_e4_lw.sh dwt_fixed       # epoch 4 from the epoch-3 checkpoint (also dwt_fixed_lw, dwt_fixed_slw)
bash scripts/run_full_dct_control.sh           # DCT without BPE, 4 epochs with the same lr history, eval after each
$PY scripts/write_reports.py codec summary
$PY scripts/write_training_report.py          # this file
